title: Analysis of Stakeholder Involvement in Nuclear Power Plant Cost Overruns and Implications for Contract Structuring
text: Analysis of Stakeholder Involvement in Nuclear Power Plant Cost Overruns and Implications for Contract Structuring. Existing evidence on nuclear power plant construction suggests that individual stakeholders involved in project delivery are often not responsible for all of the cost overruns in their scope of the project, which can lead to costly and time-consuming litigation to determine who is truly at fault for overruns. This study introduces a framework to model the share of overruns caused and received as payment by five stakeholders in a nuclear construction project: equipment suppliers, construction subcontractors, the design and management team, creditors, and the nuclear regulator. We then perform a contract analysis under three common contract structures - fixed-price, cost-plus, and performance-based - to show the profit misallocations that can result, revealing the advantages and disadvantages of each contract type for aligning stakeholder incentives. Regardless of the contract type chosen, strong owner involvement is crucial for project success, and we conclude with specific recommendations for project owners seeking to minimize cost overruns.

title: QUANTITATIVE EVALUATION OF CONTRACTING MECHANISMS FOR SHARING COST AND RISK IN NUCLEAR CONSTRUCTION
text: QUANTITATIVE EVALUATION OF CONTRACTING MECHANISMS FOR SHARING COST AND RISK IN NUCLEAR CONSTRUCTION. Nuclear construction projects have historically experienced significant cost overruns and schedule delays, increasing financial risk for utilities and limiting investment in new nuclear construction. Previous research has primarily focused on technical improvements and project management practices to reduce these risks, but comparatively less attention has been given to how contract structure distributes financial risk among project participants. This research presents a quantitative framework for evaluating the economic effects of Fixed Price, Cost-Plus, and Integrated Project Delivery (IPD) contracts for nuclear construction projects. The framework calculates stakeholder-specific net present values (NPVs) for the utility, vendor, architect/engineer (AE), and constructor by modeling project costs, schedules, stakeholder ownership, payments, operating costs, and revenue throughout the project lifecycle. The framework was demonstrated using historical nuclear projects, two sets of 1000 MWe cost and schedule test cases (base and IPD), and 250 MWe stick-built and modularized test cases. The historical cases primarily served to verify that the model responds to differences in known nuclear project characteristics. For the 1000 MWe test cases, Fixed Price generally provided the greatest protection to the utility against construction cost growth, while Cost-Plus exposed the utility to the greatest cost risk. IPD generally produced an intermediate utility response by distributing cost and schedule consequences among project participants through shared ownership and risk-reward mechanisms. The constructor, vendor, and AE experienced the opposite pattern, with greater financial exposure under Fixed Price, comparatively stable returns under Cost-Plus, and more stable but still performance dependent returns under IPD. Schedule variation primarily affected the utility through delayed operating revenue, while the other stakeholders experienced changes associated with the timing of project payments. The absence of liquidated damages in the current model limits the extent to which schedule risk is represented for non-utility stakeholders. The 250 MWe test cases further demonstrated that reactor configuration and contract structure address different aspects of nuclear project economics. The modularized reactor improved total project NPV by approximately $600 million relative to the stick-built configuration because of its lower assumed capital cost. These test cases overall saw results consistent with those found in the 1000 MWe test cases. Overall, the findings demonstrate that contract structure is an important determinant of how nuclear construction risk and economic value are distributed among project stakeholders. The results do not identify a single contract structure that produces the highest NPV for every stakeholder or project condition. Instead, it demonstrates that Fixed Price, Cost-Plus, and IPD create different risk profiles that utilities and project stakeholders can evaluate based on project characteristics and their willingness to accept project risk. The model developed provides a quantitative foundation for evaluating alternative contractual arrangements and investigating whether collaborative risk-sharing structures can improve the economic attractiveness of new nuclear construction while maintaining incentives for successful project performance.
